# Exercise 2.3 — Missing data {#sec-missing-data}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Describe the missingness in a file numerically and visually, and say how many
  rows are complete without counting them by hand.
- Decide whether a missingness pattern is plausible as something a clinic
  produced, using a comparison rather than an impression.
- Impute missing values with a stated rule, and name two properties of the data
  your imputation changed.
:::

## Why this, here

In @sec-first-look the absent values were disguised as zeros. Here they are
honest `NA`s, which removes the detective work and leaves the harder question:
once you can see the holes, what do you do about them? Describing the pattern
comes first, because the pattern decides whether filling the holes is
reasonable at all.

## A second file, and two warnings about it

`data/longisland_heart.csv` holds 200 patients and 14 columns of cardiac
assessment. Two things about it must be said before anything else.

- The outcome, `diagnosis of heart disease`, has **five** levels, not two. It
  is a severity grade. Nothing today models it, and anyone who reaches for a
  two-class method on Day 4 should come back and check this first.
- The clinical variables are **not in clinical units**. `trestbps` — resting
  blood pressure — runs from 1 to 41, and `chol` from 1 to 100. Somebody
  recoded or binned these columns and did not write down how. You cannot say
  whether an imputed `chol` of 29 is plausible, because you do not know what 29
  means.

That second point is not a flaw in the exercise. It is the ordinary state of a
teaching extract, and recognising it is part of the work.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
heart <- read_csv("data/longisland_heart.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(heart)
colSums(is.na(heart))
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
heart = pd.read_csv("data/longisland_heart.csv")
print(heart.shape)
heart.isna().sum()
```
:::

## Seeing the pattern

Counts per column do not tell you whether the gaps line up. Three views, each
answering a different question.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(naniar)
vis_miss(heart) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))
```

`vis_miss()` draws the whole frame, one cell per value. `gg_miss_upset()` goes
further and counts the *combinations* of columns that are missing together —
which is the question that matters when you are deciding whether missingness is
a single process or several.

```{r}
gg_miss_upset(heart, nsets = 6)
```

## Python

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.imshow(heart.isna().T, aspect="auto", interpolation="nearest", cmap="viridis")
ax.set_yticks(range(heart.shape[1]), heart.columns, fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Patient (row order)")
ax.set_title("Missing values (yellow)")
plt.show()
```

The pandas equivalent of counting combinations is to group by the pattern of
missingness itself and count how often each pattern occurs.

```{python}
combo = heart.isna().apply(
    lambda row: ", ".join(heart.columns[row.values]) or "(complete)", axis=1)
print(combo.value_counts().head(8).to_string())
```
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
n_missing_per_row <- rowSums(is.na(heart))
table(n_missing_per_row)
sum(n_missing_per_row == 0)
```

## Python

```{python}
n_missing_per_row = heart.isna().sum(axis=1)
print(n_missing_per_row.value_counts().sort_index())
print((n_missing_per_row == 0).sum())
```
:::

Fifty complete patients out of 200. Three quarters of the file is unusable by
any method that requires a full row, which is what most methods silently do.

## Task 1 — Decide whether a clinic could have produced this

Look again at the column counts you printed above, then build the comparison
that settles it. Simulate a frame in which 20 values are knocked out of each of
13 columns completely at random, count how many rows end up incomplete, and
repeat that a few hundred times. Compare the real file against that
distribution.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
sim_incomplete <- replicate(300, {
  m <- sapply(1:13, function(i) sample(c(rep(TRUE, ______), rep(FALSE, 180))))
  sum(rowSums(m) > 0)
})
range(sim_incomplete); mean(sim_incomplete)

observed <- sum(rowSums(is.na(heart)) > ______)
observed
c(observed = observed, low = min(sim_incomplete), high = max(sim_incomplete))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Each column needs 20 missing out of 200, so each simulated column is a shuffle
of 20 `TRUE`s and 180 `FALSE`s. A row is incomplete if it has at least one.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
set.seed(1)
sim_incomplete <- replicate(300, {
  m <- sapply(1:13, function(i) sample(c(rep(TRUE, 20), rep(FALSE, 180))))
  sum(rowSums(m) > 0)
})
range(sim_incomplete); mean(sim_incomplete)

observed <- sum(rowSums(is.na(heart)) > 0)
observed
c(observed = observed, low = min(sim_incomplete), high = max(sim_incomplete))
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
def one_sim():
    m = np.zeros((200, 13), dtype=bool)
    for j in range(13):
        m[rng.choice(200, ______, replace=False), j] = True
    return (m.sum(axis=1) > 0).sum()

sim_incomplete = np.array([one_sim() for _ in range(300)])
print(sim_incomplete.min(), sim_incomplete.max(), sim_incomplete.mean())

observed = (heart.isna().sum(axis=1) > ______).sum()
print(observed)
print(observed, sim_incomplete.min(), sim_incomplete.max())
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
def one_sim():
    m = np.zeros((200, 13), dtype=bool)
    for j in range(13):
        m[rng.choice(200, 20, replace=False), j] = True
    return (m.sum(axis=1) > 0).sum()

sim_incomplete = np.array([one_sim() for _ in range(300)])
print(sim_incomplete.min(), sim_incomplete.max(), sim_incomplete.mean())

observed = (heart.isna().sum(axis=1) > 0).sum()
print(observed)
print(observed, sim_incomplete.min(), sim_incomplete.max())
```
:::
:::
:::

Write down your conclusion in one sentence before reading the next section.

## The result that should bother you

The simulation matches. The real file has 150 incomplete rows and random
knockout produces around 150 as well, comfortably inside the simulated range.
So the row-level pattern is consistent with missing completely at random — and
that is the finding, because **no clinic produces missingness completely at
random**.

1. Every one of the 13 predictors has **exactly** 20 missing values. Not
   19, not 22. A process that loses values independently in thirteen different
   columns does not land on the same count thirteen times; the probability of
   that is vanishing. Somebody wrote a loop.
2. Compare with @sec-first-look, where every missing `triceps` was also a
   missing `insulin`. That nesting is what a real process looks like: tests are
   ordered in bundles, bundles are skipped together, and the patients they are
   skipped for are not a random sample.
3. So this file is an exercise in *mechanics*, not in *diagnosis*. Imputation
   methods are safe to practise on it precisely because the missingness is
   artificial and ignorable. Do not take that reassurance with you.

The useful habit is the one you just performed: when a pattern looks regular,
simulate the process you think produced it and check whether the data lies
inside the result.

## Task 2 — Impute, and measure what you changed

Fill the numeric gaps with the column median, then compare the standard
deviation and a correlation before and after. Median rather than mean, because
these columns are recoded and skewed; the argument for it is the same either
way.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
num_cols <- c("age", "trestbps", "chol", "thalach", "oldpeak")

heart_imp <- heart |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), ______(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

sd_before <- sd(heart$chol, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_after  <- sd(heart_imp$chol)
c(before = sd_before, after = sd_after, ratio = sd_after / sd_before)

sum(is.na(heart_imp[num_cols]))   # expect 0 to 0
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The function that returns the middle value of a vector, with `na.rm = TRUE` so
that it can be computed at all. `ifelse()` is doing the replacing; you supply
the number it replaces with.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
num_cols <- c("age", "trestbps", "chol", "thalach", "oldpeak")

heart_imp <- heart |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

sd_before <- sd(heart$chol, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_after  <- sd(heart_imp$chol)
c(before = sd_before, after = sd_after, ratio = sd_after / sd_before)

sum(is.na(heart_imp[num_cols]))   # expect 0 to 0

cor(heart$chol, heart$thalach, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor(heart_imp$chol, heart_imp$thalach)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

num_cols = ["age", "trestbps", "chol", "thalach", "oldpeak"]
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="______")
heart_imp = heart.copy()
heart_imp[num_cols] = imputer.fit_transform(heart[num_cols])

sd_before = heart["chol"].std()
sd_after = heart_imp["chol"].std()
print(sd_before, sd_after, sd_after / sd_before)

print(heart_imp[num_cols].isna().sum().sum())   # expect 0 to 0
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

num_cols = ["age", "trestbps", "chol", "thalach", "oldpeak"]
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
heart_imp = heart.copy()
heart_imp[num_cols] = imputer.fit_transform(heart[num_cols])

sd_before = heart["chol"].std()
sd_after = heart_imp["chol"].std()
print(sd_before, sd_after, sd_after / sd_before)

print(heart_imp[num_cols].isna().sum().sum())   # expect 0 to 0

print(heart[["chol", "thalach"]].corr().iloc[0, 1])
print(heart_imp[["chol", "thalach"]].corr().iloc[0, 1])
```
:::
:::
:::

Single-value imputation moves 20 patients to the exact centre of the
distribution. The standard deviation falls, every one of those patients is now
claimed to be perfectly average, and the next analysis has no way of telling
which rows were invented. The mean survives; almost nothing else does.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What `mice` adds
`mice` (multivariate imputation by chained equations) fills each gap by
predicting it from the other columns, and does the whole thing several times so
that downstream estimates can carry the uncertainty. One complete frame from it
is still a guess, but it is a guess that respects the relationships between
columns rather than flattening them.

```{r}
library(mice)
imp <- mice(heart, m = 5, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 1)
chol_imp <- complete(imp, 1)$chol
c(observed_sd = sd(heart$chol, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_imputed_sd = sd(heart_imp$chol),
  mice_sd = sd(chol_imp))
```

Use the version of this you can defend. On a file with 10% missing and a
single-value imputation, say so in the methods; on anything important, use
multiple imputation and say that.
:::

## Task 3 — Categorical columns, and the order that matters

`sex` and `cp` (chest pain type) are categories stored as numbers. Models need
them as indicator columns, and the encoder has to be given data without gaps —
otherwise "missing" silently becomes a category of its own.

Build a `ColumnTransformer` that imputes and then encodes, and check how many
columns come out. In the R version, `exclude = c(NA, NaN)` earns its place:
this file's gaps arrive as `NaN` rather than `NA`, and `factor()` would
otherwise give them a level called "NaN" and report nothing missing at all.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
# recipes does the same job in R, and you will meet it properly in @sec-leakage.
library(recipes)
heart_cat <- heart |> mutate(across(c(sex, cp), ~ factor(.x, exclude = c(NA, NaN))))

rec <- recipe(~ age + trestbps + chol + thalach + oldpeak + sex + cp,
              data = heart_cat) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(sex, cp) |>
  step_dummy(sex, cp, one_hot = ______)
baked <- bake(prep(rec), new_data = NULL)
dim(baked)
names(baked)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`one_hot` chooses between one column per level and one fewer, which is the
difference between dummy coding for a linear model and indicator coding for
everything else. Here we want one per level, as scikit-learn produced.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
library(recipes)
heart_cat <- heart |> mutate(across(c(sex, cp), ~ factor(.x, exclude = c(NA, NaN))))

rec <- recipe(~ age + trestbps + chol + thalach + oldpeak + sex + cp,
              data = heart_cat) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(sex, cp) |>
  step_dummy(sex, cp, one_hot = TRUE)
baked <- bake(prep(rec), new_data = NULL)
dim(baked)
names(baked)
```
:::
:::
## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

cat_cols = ["sex", "cp"]
cat_steps = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("encode", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)),
])
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_cols),
    ("cat", ______, cat_cols),
])
out = prep.fit_transform(heart)
print(out.shape)
print(prep.get_feature_names_out())
print(np.isnan(out).sum())   # expect 0 to 0
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

cat_cols = ["sex", "cp"]
cat_steps = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("encode", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)),
])
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_cols),
    ("cat", cat_steps, cat_cols),
])
out = prep.fit_transform(heart)
print(out.shape)
print(prep.get_feature_names_out())
print(np.isnan(out).sum())   # expect 0 to 0
```
:::
:::
:::

Now do it in the wrong order — encode first, impute afterwards — and look at
the column names. The encoder, handed a column containing `NA`, treats
"missing" as a value worth a column of its own, and you have added a predictor
that says *this patient's chest pain type was not recorded*. Sometimes that is
exactly what you want and you should say so out loud. What you must not do is
create it by accident.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
rec_wrong <- recipe(~ sex + cp, data = heart_cat) |>
  step_dummy(sex, cp, one_hot = TRUE)
baked_wrong <- bake(prep(rec_wrong), new_data = NULL)
names(baked_wrong)
colSums(is.na(baked_wrong))
```

## Python

```{python}
encoder = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)
encoder.fit(heart[["sex", "cp"]])
print(encoder.get_feature_names_out())
```
:::

The two languages fail differently, and the R failure is the safer one.
`step_dummy()` propagates the missing value into every indicator column, so the
gaps are still gaps and the next step still has to deal with them — and if you
then add `step_impute_mode()`, recipes refuses outright, because the columns it
is being asked to fill are numeric now. scikit-learn produces `sex_nan` and
`cp_nan`: no missing values, no warning, and two extra predictors nobody asked
for.

## Reflection

1. You imputed `chol` with its median without knowing what the units are. Name
   one thing that could be wrong with the imputed values that you would be
   unable to detect.
2. Multiple imputation gives five different filled-in datasets. If the five
   disagree about an answer you care about, what does that disagreement tell
   you, and what would you report?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values.** Every predictor has exactly 20 missing (10%); 150 of 200
rows incomplete, 50 complete. The simulated range for incomplete rows is about
134–164 with a mean near 149, so the observed 150 sits in the middle. Median
imputation of `chol` drops its standard deviation by roughly 5% (ratio about
0.94–0.96); the `chol`–`thalach` correlation moves towards zero. `mice` returns
a standard deviation close to the observed one. The Python design matrix comes
out with 5 numeric columns plus one indicator per level of `sex` and `cp`.

**Task 1 is the point of the exercise.** The evidence students should name is
"exactly 20 in every column", not the simulation — the simulation only rules
out the alternative that the regularity is a coincidence of the row structure.
A student who says "it is MCAR, so it is fine" has drawn the wrong conclusion
and should be asked what clinical process would do this.

**Reflection 1.** The median is a plausible value, but plausibility is
unverifiable when the scale is unknown: if `chol` is a binned percentile, the
median is not the median cholesterol of anyone. Accept any answer that
distinguishes *numerically reasonable* from *clinically meaningful*.

**Common failures.** (1) `median(.x)` without `na.rm = TRUE`, which returns
`NA` and imputes nothing — the check catches it. (2) `gg_miss_upset()` errors if
`naniar` is not installed; `vis_miss()` alone is enough. (3) Running the Python
`ColumnTransformer` cell before `num_cols` exists, because they skipped Task 2.

**Timing.** The simulation in Task 1 takes longer to explain than to run. If
you are behind, give them the simulated range verbally and spend the time on
Task 3, which is the one that shows up again in @sec-leakage.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Is missingness informative here?
Add a column `chol_missing` and test whether it is associated with the outcome
grade. In this file it should not be, by construction. Run the same test on
`insulin_missing` in `data/diabetes.csv` and compare. One of these files is
teaching you mechanics and the other is teaching you suspicion.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Pool, do not pick
Fit the same simple model on each of the five `mice` completions and look at
how much the coefficient for one predictor moves between them. That spread is
the part single imputation throws away. `pool()` is the function that combines
them properly.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can describe a missingness pattern in numbers and in a
picture, that you tested a hypothesis about how it arose rather than asserting
one, and that you can impute and state what the imputation cost.

**Cannot:** that any of this was done safely. Every statistic you used to fill
a gap — a median, a mode, a `mice` model — was computed from the whole file,
including the rows you will later use to test a model. That is @sec-leakage,
and it is the reason today is built this way.
